= Affirmation-check trust material

`github-web-flow.gpg` in this directory is GitHub's *current* web-flow
commit-signing public key:

* fingerprint: `9684 79A1 AFF9 27E3 7D1A 566B B569 0EEE BB95 2194`
* created 2024-01-16, no expiry
* fetched 2026-10-28 from `gh api users/web-flow/gpg_keys`
  (the entry with `key_id` `B5690EEEBB952194`)

`github-web-flow-previous.gpg` is the expired key it replaced
(`5DE3E0509C47EA3CF04A42D34AEE18F83AFDEB23`), kept so historical commits can
still be classified.

== Why it exists

The Affirmation Document Gate (`actions/affirmation-check`) attempts to classify
the signature on the commit that last changed `AFFIRMATION.adoc`, using the
available Git history. The copy of the web-flow key vendored inside that action
is GitHub's *previous* key
(`5DE3E0509C47EA3CF04A42D34AEE18F83AFDEB23`, expired 2024-01-16) — the action's
own fingerprint allowlist names the new key, but the new key is not in its
keyring. A GitHub-signed commit whose key the keyring lacks (web merges, squash
landings, and the test-merge commit a shallow PR checkout consists of)
classifies as `E` ("cannot be checked"), which the action treats as "bad,
revoked, or failed verification" and fails on. That was the `estate-audit`
failure on PR #102.

`check.sh` in this directory is that action's script vendored from
`cicd-suite@bf7dd95cf49733019343ff485c2f45c6b261839c` with a local repair: `E`
accompanied by GnuPG's `NO_PUBKEY` is a notice; bad, revoked, and other failed
verifications still fail. The local script imports both the current and
historical vendored GitHub keys and rejects them unless their primary
fingerprints match the two pinned above.

== Current status (2026-11-09)

`main-estate-audit.yml` is now a thin caller of the suite's shared reusable
workflow, so the gate that runs on this repository is *upstream's*
`actions/affirmation-check` at the suite's own pin — not the local script. The
local script is no longer wired into CI.

That gate checks out at depth 1, so the commit whose signature it classifies is
the *checkout boundary*. On a pull request that is the test-merge commit; on a
push it is the branch tip. Neither is necessarily the commit that last changed
`AFFIRMATION.adoc`. The gate emits a notice naming the boundary commit. Even
when that commit's signature verifies, CI may not have checked the signature
on the commit that last changed `AFFIRMATION.adoc`. A passing gate can also
report that the boundary commit's signature could not be verified.
Measured on this repository 2026-11-09: the gate passes in both shapes
(`estate-audit / governance` on PR run 42605863386; a depth-1 push-shape run
over the GitHub-signed landing commit `c0eb4f1` exited 0 with "verified with a
trusted key: GitHub <noreply@github.com>"), and it classifies the boundary
commit in both.

The local script is kept because:

* it is the reference implementation of the fix the upstream action still
  needs. Re-checked 2026-11-09: the suite's vendored `github-web-flow.gpg` is
  byte-identical to `github-web-flow-previous.gpg` here — its only key is the
  2017 primary `5DE3E050…`, not the 2024 key `968479A1…` that signed this
  repository's recent landings. Upstream's verification of those landings
  therefore depends on resolving a key that is not in the file it ships (it
  succeeded on the runner, which has network), which is precisely the fragile
  path the local repair hardens: it ships both keys and turns a `NO_PUBKEY`
  into a notice instead of a failure;
* `tests/workflows/review_regressions_test.sh` exercises it, so the repair
  cannot rot silently;
* if the shared gate ever starts failing on a key it cannot classify, this
  script is the local oracle to diagnose it — run
  `bash .github/affirmation-trusted/check.sh` from the repository root.

This was always a contained workaround, not the durable trust boundary: gate
code in a pull-request checkout is necessarily reviewed code, and the root fix
belongs upstream. If GitHub rotates the web-flow key again, re-fetch it the
same way and update the fingerprint above in the same commit.
